answer.label: No documented source — credited to Louis Armstrong without evidence
answer.authorName: Unknown — not documented as Louis Armstrong
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is widely pinned to Louis Armstrong, yet it appears in none of his autobiographies, letters, or recorded interviews, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s Armstrong page entirely. It surfaces only on modern quote-aggregator and fan sites, none of which cite a source — so there is no evidence Armstrong said it, and its true originator is unknown.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Modern quote-aggregator sites; no dated attestation found

source.excerpt: Musicians don’t retire; they stop when there’s no more music in them.
trail: The line is carried by quote sites such as BrainyQuote and Goodreads, none of which name a source — Goodreads notes its quotes are community-added and “not verified.”
Even the fan-run Louis Armstrong Society lists the line without any citation, date, or provenance.
It does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Armstrong page — not in the Sourced section, nor among Reputed or Misattributed quotes — and Quote Investigator has no entry for it.
Armstrong is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good sayings; consistency with his life story is not the same as a documented source.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced as it circulates online. No primary source — book, letter, interview, or broadcast — has been located for this wording.
source.rightsNote: Because no source work or first-publication can be identified for this wording, its copyright status cannot be determined. It is treated as of uncertain rights — no public-domain claim is asserted for an aphorism whose origin is unknown.

author.name: Louis Armstrong
author.heading: About Louis Armstrong
author.metaLine: 1901–1971 · American jazz trumpeter & vocalist · New Orleans
author.bio: Louis “Satchmo” Armstrong was one of the most influential figures in jazz, a virtuoso trumpeter and gravel-voiced vocalist whose career ran from 1920s Chicago and New York into worldwide stardom. He kept performing almost to the end of his life, playing despite heart trouble and his doctors’ warnings — the very quality that makes this unsourced line feel plausibly his. He died in Queens, New York, in July 1971.

misattribution.heading: An unsourced line pinned to a magnet name
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Louis Armstrong rests entirely on repetition across quote sites, with no underlying document ever cited.

items.why: No autobiography, letter, interview transcript, or broadcast has been found containing this sentence, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s curated Armstrong page. The credit appears only on aggregator and fan pages such as BrainyQuote, none of which name a source.

Armstrong famously kept performing despite ill health, so the sentiment is in character — but a plausible fit is not evidence he coined this phrasing, and no earlier speaker has been identified either.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that no one has shown where this line comes from: it reads as a modern inspirational saying of unknown authorship, attached to Armstrong because famous names sell quotes. See Wikiquote for what he is actually documented to have said.

context.heading: Why the credit sticks
lead: Louis Armstrong is a prime target for orphaned aphorisms: he is warm, universally known, and bound up with a life story — playing his trumpet nearly until his death in 1971 — that makes almost any line about music and perseverance feel like something he might have said. That plausibility is exactly what lets an unsourced sentence travel for years without anyone asking for a citation.

This particular line has all the marks of a later, anonymous inspirational quote: clean parallel structure, no awkward period detail, and a first appearance on quote-aggregator pages rather than in any interview, memoir, or news report. Until a dated primary source turns up, the accurate label is ‘origin unknown.’
context.pull: In character is not the same as on the record.
